name: Facial acupuncture (cosmetic acupuncture)

lead:
Facial acupuncture (also called cosmetic acupuncture) applies very thin needles to points on the face, scalp and neck, often with body points as well. People use it hoping for fewer visible fine lines, firmer-looking skin, a brighter complexion and, in some studies, lighter melasma patches.
The appearance payoff is argued to come from stimulating skin and facial muscle tone and local circulation. Published studies, including randomized trials on frown lines and melasma, report improvements in photographed wrinkles or pigment area, but many are small, open-label or use no sham group.

paras: Sessions are given by a trained acupuncturist. Studies typically use a course of treatments once or twice a week over four to eight weeks, with needles placed in the face, head and neck and sometimes body points. Practitioners often present it as a series rather than a single visit, and results in trials were assessed from photographs and satisfaction scales a few weeks afterwards.

Reported effects include bruising and minor bleeding at needle sites. Case reports describe rarer complications after cosmetic facial acupuncture, including a facial skin reaction (sclerosing lipogranulomatosis) and a deep infection of the infratemporal fossa. Non-sterile technique and unlicensed practitioners raise infection risk; people with bleeding disorders or skin infections are generally advised to discuss it with a clinician first.

angle.text: People use a course of cosmetic acupuncture sessions to soften the look of frown lines and nasolabial folds and to even skin tone. Trials measure the result from standardized photographs and satisfaction scores a few weeks after treatment.

lead: Facial acupuncture, also known as cosmetic acupuncture, is a form of acupuncture in which fine needles are inserted into the face, head and neck, frequently alongside points on the body, with the aim of improving how the skin and face look. It is marketed as a non-surgical option for wrinkles, skin texture, facial elasticity and uneven pigmentation, and is sometimes grouped with facial exercises and facial acupressure as a non-medical approach to facial rejuvenation [1].

People who use it usually book a course of sessions with an acupuncturist and track changes in lines around the forehead, nasolabial folds and overall skin tone. Practitioners describe the mechanism as restoring resting tone of facial muscles and stimulating the skin, a hypothesis stated explicitly by the authors of a Korean pilot study of facial elasticity [2].

Research consists mainly of small trials. A randomized wait-list trial in Iran of 72 women reported reduced frown lines after body and facial acupuncture [3], a Thai randomized trial found smaller melasma areas with facial acupuncture [4], and single-arm studies in Korea and China reported improvements in elasticity and wrinkle scores [2][5]. Case reports also document complications of the procedure [6][7].

paras: Facial acupuncture borrows the needling techniques of traditional Chinese medicine and applies them to areas of the face with an aesthetic goal. Published protocols name points such as those near the eyebrows, cheeks, nasolabial folds and temples, with some trials combining them with body points [3][5]. A variant described in a Chinese study, termed stuck acupuncture, threads needles between facial points and was combined with conventional facial acupuncture [5].

Trials have examined three main targets: frown lines, nasolabial folds and marionette lines, and melasma. A retrospective study of 100 beauty-seeking patients compared two distinct acupuncture techniques for nasolabial folds and marionette lines [8]. Melasma has been studied with facial acupuncture alone, with body points added, and combined with auricular acupressure [4][9].
A 2014 systematic review of non-medical facial rejuvenation approaches covered facial exercises rather than needling, and noted that studies in that field lacked control groups and randomization [1].

In a 2016 Thai randomized trial, 41 women with melasma received facial acupuncture or facial plus body acupuncture twice weekly for eight weeks; melasma area decreased in 90 percent and 95 percent of the two groups respectively, with a mean reduction of about 2.4 to 2.6 cm2 [4].

A 2025 randomized wait-list trial of 72 women aged 30-59 compared facial and body acupuncture twice weekly for six weeks with no treatment. At week 7, 63 percent of treated participants showed reduced frown lines at rest and 72 percent on maximal frowning, and gains were largely maintained at week 12 [3].

A 2025 Chinese study of 22 women using stuck and facial acupuncture for four weeks reported lower wrinkle severity, texture and pore scores, with 3 complete and 15 obvious improvements [5]. A 2013 open-label single-arm pilot in Korea examined facial elasticity [2], and a 2012 preliminary study in Acupuncture in Medicine examined facial skin appearance [10]. Tools such as a Facial Check Sheet have been validated to measure self-satisfaction with cosmetic acupuncture [11].
Most of these studies have small samples and several have no sham-needle comparison, so the size of any effect beyond placebo and wait-list conditions remains to be established.

Case reports describe a dermatologic complication, extensive facial sclerosing lipogranulomatosis, following cosmetic acupuncture [6], and an infratemporal fossa abscess after facial acupuncture, which the authors attributed to infection risk in the face [7]. Bruising at needle sites is a commonly noted effect of facial needling in general.

Facial acupuncture appears on the fringe of appearance communities alongside facial exercise and microneedling as a needle-based option for skin quality and facial tone. Discussion in the forums is sparse and mostly concerns acupuncture generally rather than cosmetic use.
